facts.title: Born in a Berkeley Cyclotron
facts.text: Californium was first created in 1950 at the University of California, Berkeley, by Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street Jr., Albert Ghiorso, and Glenn Seaborg. They produced it by bombarding a tiny target of curium-242 with alpha particles in the 60-inch cyclotron. The very first batch contained only about 5,000 atoms, far too few to see, yet enough to identify a brand-new element.

facts.title: Named for a State and a School
facts.text: The element honors both the U.S. state of California and the University of California. The discoverers noted with some humor that, unlike earlier explorers who had to cross an ocean to reach California, scientists searching for element 98 faced the much harder journey of crossing the periodic table. It remains one of the few elements named after a specific university.

facts.title: A Neutron Factory in Your Hand
facts.text: One microgram of californium-252 spits out about 2.3 million neutrons every second through spontaneous fission. This makes it one of the most powerful portable neutron sources known, with no reactor or accelerator required. A single gram would release roughly 2.3 trillion neutrons per second, a staggering output for a speck of metal.

facts.title: Finding Gold and Oil Underground
facts.text: Because it floods its surroundings with neutrons, Cf-252 is used in well-logging tools that scan rock formations for oil, water, and minerals. The neutrons interact with atoms in the rock, and the returning radiation reveals what lies underground. The same neutron flood is used in portable scanners that detect gold, silver, and even explosives or landmines.

facts.title: Jump-Starting Nuclear Reactors
facts.text: Californium-252 serves as a reliable startup neutron source for nuclear reactors, providing the initial burst of neutrons needed to kick off a controlled chain reaction. It is also used to calibrate radiation detectors and to study how materials behave under intense neutron bombardment. Its predictable, steady neutron output makes it ideal for these precise jobs.

facts.title: Treating Cancer With Neutrons
facts.text: In medicine, californium-252 has been used in brachytherapy, where tiny sealed sources are placed inside or next to a tumor. The neutrons it emits can damage cancer cells that resist ordinary X-ray and gamma-ray treatments, including some cervical, brain, and oral cancers. This makes it a valuable option for certain hard-to-treat tumors.

facts.title: Among the Most Expensive Substances
facts.text: Californium is extraordinarily costly to make, with prices historically quoted around 27 million U.S. dollars per gram for Cf-252. Only fractions of a gram are produced worldwide each year, chiefly at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee and at a reactor in Dimitrovgrad, Russia. This scarcity places it among the priciest materials on Earth by weight.

facts.title: It Glows From Its Own Decay
facts.text: A concentrated sample of californium is so intensely radioactive that it actually glows, heated by the energy of its own constant decay. The radiation is hazardous enough that it can disrupt the formation of red blood cells in the body if mishandled. Researchers must handle it remotely behind heavy shielding using glove boxes and robotic arms.

facts.title: Heavier Cousins Owe It Thanks
facts.text: Californium is one of the few elements heavy enough to serve as a target for making even more exotic elements. Bombarding Cf-249 with calcium-48 ions was the method used to synthesize oganesson, element 118, the heaviest element currently known. Without enough californium to build a target, the bottom row of the periodic table could not have been completed.

facts.title: Glimpsed in an Exploding Star
facts.text: Californium does not occur naturally on Earth in any meaningful amount, since its longest-lived isotope, Cf-251, has a half-life of only about 900 years. However, its telltale signature was reported in the light of supernovae, where the violent collapse and explosion of dying stars can briefly forge such heavy elements. Studying these signatures helps astronomers understand how nature builds the heaviest atoms.
